reference.en:
Finish the note and the caution in it is right: National Logistics should treat the two trucks as costing the same to own and decide between them on non-financial grounds — it should not buy hybrids expecting a $9,000 saving.

The fuel line is correct and it is not the answer. The hybrid does burn $9,000 a year less — 6,000 gallons against 3,000 at $3.00 — but the rows the note never converted absorb exactly that: depreciation is $5,000 higher, because $150,000 over ten years is $15,000 against $100,000 over ten years; maintenance is $3,000 higher; insurance is $1,000 higher. Add owning to running and both trucks land on the same annual figure, $35,000.

Two things could break that and only one of them survives contact with the data. The idea that the hybrid outlives the diesel and so carries less depreciation is closed off by the exhibit — both lifespans are ten years, and salvage value is zero, so nothing comes back at the end. Rising fuel prices are a real exposure and I want to be honest that the case does not settle them: we are told prices have been climbing, but no future price is given. What I can size is the sensitivity — the gap in consumption is 3,000 gallons, so every sustained dollar per gallon is $3,000 a year per truck in the hybrid's favour. On the printed $3.00 it is a dead heat.

So: buy on service life, driver retention, emissions exposure or maintenance terms, not on a fuel saving. Before the next replacement cycle I would put a contracted diesel price and a quoted hybrid service and insurance package in front of the client — those three lines are what the tie is made of — and I would spend the cost-reduction effort where the numbers are not tied, which is the driver wage line the client opened with.

**Built number [BUILD]** — BUILT — the book does not print it

```python
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

D = Decimal
def r0(x): return x.quantize(D("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)

# --- everything below is from the book: EXHIBIT 1 (p. 52) + the depreciation rule (p. 53) ---
MILES       = D("60000")
FUEL_PRICE  = D("3.00")
std = {"price": D("100000"), "maint": D("5000"), "ins": D("2000"), "mpg": D("10"), "life": D("10")}
hyb = {"price": D("150000"), "maint": D("8000"), "ins": D("3000"), "mpg": D("20"), "life": D("10")}

def gallons(t):  return MILES / t["mpg"]
def annual(t, price_per_gal):
    dep  = t["price"] / t["life"]          # straight-line, $0 salvage
    fuel = gallons(t) * price_per_gal
    return t["maint"] + t["ins"] + dep + fuel

# book check (book figures, p. 53, Answer block)
assert gallons(std) == D("6000") and gallons(hyb) == D("3000")
assert r0(annual(std, FUEL_PRICE)) == D("35000")
assert r0(annual(hyb, FUEL_PRICE)) == D("35000")
assert r0(annual(std, FUEL_PRICE) - annual(hyb, FUEL_PRICE)) == D("0")

# decomposition: the fuel saving is eaten by exactly three items
fuel_saving = gallons(std) * FUEL_PRICE - gallons(hyb) * FUEL_PRICE
dep_penalty = hyb["price"]/hyb["life"] - std["price"]/std["life"]
mnt_penalty = hyb["maint"] - std["maint"]
ins_penalty = hyb["ins"]   - std["ins"]
assert fuel_saving == D("9000")
assert (dep_penalty, mnt_penalty, ins_penalty) == (D("5000"), D("3000"), D("1000"))
assert dep_penalty + mnt_penalty + ins_penalty == fuel_saving

# --- BUILT — the book does not print it: sensitivity to the fuel price ---
# consumption gap = 3,000 gallons/year -> every +$1/gallon = $3,000/year in favour of the hybrid
gallon_gap = gallons(std) - gallons(hyb)
assert gallon_gap == D("3000")
per_dollar = gallon_gap * D("1.00")
assert per_dollar == D("3000")          # $/year per tractor for every +$1/gallon

# break-even fuel price: standard - hybrid = -9000 + 3000*p = 0
breakeven_price = (mnt_penalty + ins_penalty + dep_penalty) / gallon_gap
assert breakeven_price == D("3")        # the tie sits exactly on the printed $3.00 price
assert r0(annual(std, D("4.00")) - annual(hyb, D("4.00"))) == D("3000")
```

**Provoked error** — to step over the caveat in the truncated note, take a correctly computed saving on one line ($9,000 on fuel) for the saving on the total, and fail to build the three offsetting items ($5,000 depreciation + $3,000 maintenance + $1,000 insurance), which cancel it exactly.

**[TWO LEVERS]** Lever 1 — the fuel price, which the record already moves: the consumption gap is 6,000 gallons against 3,000, so every sustained dollar per gallon is $3,000 a year per tractor in the hybrid's favour, and at the printed $3.00 the two trucks tie at $35,000 a year each. Lever 2 — annual mileage, the 60,000 miles that produce that 3,000-gallon gap in the first place. Move both, using only printed inputs. The hybrid's fixed penalty is $9,000 a year: depreciation $5,000 ($150,000 / 10 against $100,000 / 10), maintenance $3,000 and insurance $1,000. The fuel gap is 1/10 - 1/20 = 0.05 gallons a mile, so at $3.00 it is $0.15 a mile and break-even mileage is $9,000 / $0.15 = 60,000 miles — exactly the figure printed in the exhibit. At $4.00 a gallon the gap is $0.20 a mile and break-even falls to $9,000 / $0.20 = 45,000 miles, so any tractor running under 45,000 miles a year still favours the diesel even at that price. What survives: the verdict. At the printed inputs both trucks cost $35,000 a year to own and run, lifespans are both ten years with $0 salvage so nothing comes back at the end, and the choice has to be made on service life, driver retention, emissions exposure or maintenance terms. What does not survive: the tie as a one-parameter fact. It is doubly conditional, so a contracted diesel price alone does not settle it — the client also needs the mileage distribution across the 90-truck fleet, and the record prints only a single 60,000-mile average.

drills.anchor_metric: Клиентского порога нет; решение выносится сопоставлением двух колонок, а не сравнением с правилом. Вердикт держится тем, что обе колонки дают одну и ту же годовую сумму

drills.title: A Billion Short
drills.family_note: круг 34, ревью: заявлялась F8 и не подтвердилась — наивный и decoy ведут к «не запускать», верный к «запускать», это разворот. Реальная механика — тестом объявлена не та величина, по которой считает записка: подмена базы решения.
drills.anchor_metric: programme surplus, $B
drills.prompt:
A programme office has been asked whether the state should distribute insurance through the postal network to the two underserved social classes. An analyst has already worked the numbers and left the working note below, together with the brief he was given. The steering committee meets in ten minutes and wants a verdict from you.

**Give your answer in two fields: conclusion first, then everything else.**

exhibit.title: Analyst's working note — postal insurance programme

lines: **Block A — size of the two target classes**
Midpoint income taken as representative. Aspirers: $15K × 80M × 1.5% = **$18B**. Strugglers: $5K × 120M × 1% = **$6B**. Two classes together = **$24B**.
**Block B — what we would actually capture in three years**
66% of Strugglers and 33% of Aspirers: 0.66 × $6B + 0.33 × $18B ≈ $4B + $6B = **$10B** of premium.
**Block C — what it costs**
The network has 150,000 post offices; two-thirds of them can hire one agent — 100,000 agents.
Agent payroll $15,000 each = **$1.5B**. Agent commission 10% of premium = **$1.0B**. Operating cost $5,000 per post office = **$0.5B**. Claims paid out at 80% of premium = **$8.0B**.
**Block D — where I got to**

Premium in $10.0B, cost out $11.0B. The programme runs a **$1.0B deficit** in its first three years. I have not been able to find a version of the rollout that closes it: dropping agents cuts reach faster than it cuts cost, and the claims ratio is the actuarial floor, not a lever.
I stopped here and did not write a recommendation.
**Block E — the brief I was issued, attached for the file**
"Primary objective is not to monetize insurance offerings, but instead to improve quality of life by providing insurance-based safety nets. However, profitability is seen as an important metric."
Insurance here covers both life and non-life — health, crop and so on.

key.naive: **Naive path — the honest first answer of a clever person.** Read Block E as the answer: a $1.0B hole with no closing move, therefore do not launch, or launch only after the economics are fixed. Every number on that path is right. The arithmetic is not where this slot is decided.
key.decoy: **The tempting second branch.** Redesign for break-even before rollout — fewer post offices, lower commission, tighter underwriting. It reads as the responsible middle. It is the same refusal wearing a plan: every lever that closes $1.0B removes coverage, and coverage is the objective.
key.support: **What decides it, and all of it is in Block A.** The brief names the objective in its first sentence — safety nets, not monetisation — and demotes profitability to "an important metric", not the test. Against that objective the programme delivers $10.0B of premium-equivalent protection to the two classes with the least of it, at a net public cost of $1.0B. **[ПОСТРОЕНО, книга не печатает]** on the note's own rounded figures that is a subsidy of 10.0% of the protection delivered ($1.0B ÷ $10.0B); on the unrounded chain it is 10.2%. The verdict does not turn on a better number; it turns on which number was ever the test.
key.correct: Proceed with the rollout as scoped.
key.risks: Internal: the 80% claims ratio is an assumption, and a 5 pp move is **[ПОСТРОЕНО]** ±$0.5B on a $1.0B deficit — the figure the committee is being asked to accept is only as firm as that ratio. External: the book's own two — excessive load on the medical system, and moral hazard once coverage is free at the point of sale.
key.next: Name the $1.0B as a budgeted public-health line before launch, not as an overrun found later. Test whether a larger captured share of the same two classes narrows it, and price-test programmes that widen access without adding cost.

en: Minto: the first sentence is the verdict itself — an action with a subject ("the government should proceed"). A correct verdict that arrives after the facts fails this line.
States that the objective in Block A, not the surplus in Block E, is the test.
Names the $1.0B deficit out loud rather than avoiding it — the answer is that it is a price, not that it is absent.
Uses at least two figures from the note: $10.0B captured and $11.0B cost, or the $24B market against them.
Gives one internal and one external risk.
Does not invent a lever that closes the gap; the note already ruled the obvious ones out.
ru: Минто: первое предложение — сам вердикт, действием и с субъектом. Верный вывод, приехавший после фактов, не засчитывается.
Сказано, что тестом является цель из блока A, а не сальдо из блока E.
Дефицит $1.0B назван вслух: ответ в том, что это цена, а не в том, что его нет.
Использованы минимум две величины записи: $10.0B захвата и $11.0B издержек.
Назван один внутренний и один внешний риск.
Не выдуман рычаг, закрывающий дыру — записка уже перебрала очевидные.

reference.en:
| field | text |
|---|---|
| **conclusion** | **The government should proceed with the postal insurance rollout as scoped.** |
| **the rest** | The brief makes safety-net coverage the objective and profitability only an important metric, so the $1.0B gap is the price of the objective, not evidence against it. On the numbers the programme reaches the two least-covered classes with **$10.0B** of premium against **$11.0B** of cost, and every lever that closes the gap — fewer post offices, lower commission, tighter underwriting — removes the coverage that is the point. **[BUILT — the book does not print it]** the deficit is 10.0% of the protection delivered on the note's rounded figures, 10.2% unrounded. Risks: internally the 80% claims ratio is an assumption and 5 pp of it is ±$0.5B, which is half the deficit; externally the load on the medical system and moral hazard. Next: carry the $1.0B as a budgeted public-health line rather than an overrun, and test whether a larger captured share of the same two classes narrows it. |

**Source:** `Wharton Casebook 23-24`, Case 13 The Claim Game, pp. 151–158 — prompt block, Additional Information block, Exhibit A, Math blocks, Recommendation block.

**[TWO LEVERS]** Lever 1 — the claims ratio, which the record already moves: claims run at 80% of premium and 5 percentage points is plus or minus $500,000,000 on $10,000,000,000 of captured premium, half the $1,000,000,000 deficit. Lever 2 — the agent commission, printed at 10% of premium and worth $1,000,000,000 in Block C. Move both by the same 5 percentage points. Downward: claims to 75% releases $500,000,000 and commission to 5% releases another $500,000,000; together that is $1,000,000,000 and the programme breaks exactly even at $11,000,000,000 of cost falling to $10,000,000,000. Upward: claims at 85% and commission at 15% add $1,000,000,000 and the deficit doubles to $2,000,000,000. What survives: the verdict. The brief makes safety-net coverage the objective and profitability only an important metric, the programme reaches the two least-covered classes with $10,000,000,000 of premium out of a $24,000,000,000 market, and every lever that closes the gap removes the coverage that is the point. What does not survive: $1,000,000,000 as a fixed price. Across two 5 percentage point moves the band is $0 to $2,000,000,000 — the full size of the number itself — and the commission half of that band is the very lever the note ruled out, because dropping agents cuts reach faster than it cuts cost. Break-even is therefore reachable, but only by paying for it in coverage, which is why the recommendation carries the gap as a budgeted public-health line rather than closing it.

drills.title: Seven Cents A Cup
drills.family_note: круг 38: вторая ветвь (ответить ценой) — только соблазн; честный ответ — продолжать делать то же самое, и это разворота не даёт
drills.anchor_metric: net margin per cup, cents
drills.prompt:
A national supplier of foam cups to restaurant chains has a new competitor: an importer selling at a lower price. An associate has been through the numbers and the customer survey and left the working note below. He has drafted a response but not a verdict.

**Answer in two fields: conclusion first, then everything else.**

exhibit.title: Associate's working note — response to the new entrant

lines: **Block A — unit economics, cents per cup**
Our cost is 4 + 3 = **7**, so we keep **3** of every 10 — a **30%** net margin.
The entrant's cost is 4 + 3 + 2 = **9** against a price of **7**: they are **2 cents under water on every cup** and have been from the day they arrived.
**Block B — what matching would do**
If we go to their price of 7, our cost of 7 leaves **0**. The whole 3 cents goes, and we would be selling at cost against an importer who is already selling below it.
**Block C — customer survey, what buyers weigh**

Buyers were asked to rank what matters when choosing a supplier. **Service reliability comes first, well ahead of price; design comes last.** On the reliability score we are rated materially above the entrant.
**Block D — the response I drafted**

A staged price move: down 1 cent now as a signal to the accounts most at risk, a second cent if the entrant holds his price into next quarter, and contract lock-ins negotiated in parallel. It costs a third of our margin in year one and it answers the attack directly.
I have not written the recommendation.

key.naive: **Naive path — the honest first answer.** A cheaper competitor has arrived, so the response is priced: match partly, signal to the accounts at risk, lock in contracts. Block D is a competent plan, and every number in it is right. It is what an experienced person drafts when the trigger is a price.
key.decoy: **The tempting second branch — and it is not the staged cut, it is the lock-in.** Sign the at-risk accounts to long contracts now, while the entrant is cheap and we still look safe. It costs nothing this quarter and feels like defence. It also fixes our price into the one period when the entrant's 2-cent burn is most likely to end, and it buys loyalty on the attribute the survey ranks below reliability — spending the negotiation on price when the thing we win on is service.
key.support: **What decides it, and it is Block C against Block A.** The attack is on the attribute buyers rank last-but-one, while the attribute they rank first is the one we already win. Meanwhile the entrant is 2 cents under water per cup, so his price is not a position he holds, it is a burn he funds — and matching it would take us from 3 cents to 0 while he is still below us. There is no version of the price branch that leaves us better off than doing nothing to price at all.
key.correct: Hold the price and spend on reliability instead.
key.risks: Internal: the whole verdict rests on the survey ranking, and a survey is a snapshot — if reliability stops being the first-ranked attribute the answer changes. External: the book's own — price becomes a pain point if the economy turns, and a buyer under cost pressure re-ranks fast.
key.next: Put the reliability lead under measurement rather than assertion — on-time delivery by account — and watch the entrant's price for the point at which he stops funding the 2-cent gap.

en: Minto: the first sentence is the verdict itself, an action with a subject ("we should hold price"). A correct verdict arriving after the facts fails this line.
States that the attacked attribute is not the one buyers rank first — the survey is used, not just mentioned.
Names what matching costs: 3 cents to 0, that is the whole margin.
Names that the entrant is loss-making at 2 cents per cup, so the low price is funded, not sustainable.
Rejects the staged version explicitly, not only the full match.
Gives one internal and one external risk.
ru: Минто: первое предложение — сам вердикт, действием и с субъектом. Верный вывод после фактов не засчитывается.
Сказано, что атакуют не тот атрибут, который покупатель ставит первым: опрос использован, а не упомянут.
Названа цена совпадения по цене: 3 цента превращаются в 0, то есть вся маржа.
Названо, что вошедший убыточен на 2 цента с чашки — его цена финансируется, а не держится.
Отвергнута именно ступенчатая версия, а не только полное совпадение.
Назван один внутренний и один внешний риск.

reference.en:
| field | text |
|---|---|
| **conclusion** | **We should hold our price and put the money into service reliability instead.** |
| **the rest** | The attack is on price, and price is not what buyers decide on: the survey ranks service reliability first and design last, and reliability is where we are rated materially above the entrant. Matching costs everything we have — our cost is **7** against a price of **10**, so going to **7** takes the margin from **3 cents to 0** — and it would be a concession made to a competitor who is **2 cents under water on every cup** and funding that gap rather than holding a position. The staged version in Block D is the same concession slowed down: it accepts price as the field. Risks: internally the verdict rests on a survey ranking, which is a snapshot; externally price becomes a pain point if the economy turns. Next: measure the reliability lead by on-time delivery per account rather than asserting it, and watch for the point at which the entrant stops funding the 2-cent gap. |

**Source:** `Darden 2019` (2018-19 Casebook), Styrofoam Situation, pp. 58–67 — Exhibit 1 unit economics (10 / 7 price; 4 manufacturing, 3 shipping, 2 distribution), the Exhibit 1 guidance block ("net margin is 30%", "Chalice Inc is running at a loss", "All of Cup Co's profit will be eroded if they try to match"), the Exhibit 2 guidance block ("The most important metric to customers is reliability of service and Cup Co ranks a lot higher"), and the Conclusion block ("Cup Co should not lower its price").

drills.title: The Model That Won Last Year
drills.family_note: круг 41: ранжирование верно для того года, в котором посчитано, и неверно для горизонта, на который принимается решение — рамка сменилась не в записи, а между записью и решением
drills.anchor_metric: first-year profit by revenue model, $M
drills.prompt:
Kelvarno is choosing the revenue model for a subscription app before launch. An analyst has priced all three and left the note below. Give your verdict.

**One field, free text. Put the block markers in yourself.**

lines: **Block A — addressable base**
6,000,000 potential users.
**Block B — first-year economics of each model**
Fixed costs $10,000,000 a year in every case; variable operating cost $1 per member per year, already deducted above.
**Block C — the market series I was also given**

The share of users in this category who pay a monthly fee, and the average fee they pay, have been falling since 2008, and the fall steepens from 2013. Free competitors with the same core features arrived in late 2012 and the shift to them has not slowed since.
**Block D — where I got to**

On first-year profit the monthly fee wins: **$25.7M** against **$20.6M** and **$16.4M**, a lead of **$5.1M** over the next model. I have priced all three the same way and on the same base. I did not write a recommendation.

key.naive: **Naive path — and it is the honest one.** Take the ranking as computed: monthly fee earns $5.1M more in year one than premium, the arithmetic is identical across the three models, so pick the monthly fee. Nothing in Block B is wrong, and a careful person checks Block B and stops there.
key.decoy: **The tempting second branch.** Launch on the monthly fee and switch later, when the decline bites. It sounds like optionality and it is the opposite: the fee model takes 5% of the base onto the platform, the premium model takes 30% — switching later means switching a base six times smaller, built on the promise that made it pay.
key.support: **What decides it is Block C, and Block C is not about this year.** The choice is made once and lived with for years, while the $25.7M is a first-year figure computed on a share of payers that is falling and a fee that is falling with it. The premium model is behind by **$5.1M** on a year that already happened by the time the decision matters, and it stands on **1,800,000** users against **300,000** — the model that survives the trend is the one whose base is not the shrinking segment.
key.correct: Launch on the premium-account model, not the monthly fee.
key.risks: Internal: premium conversion is itself an assumption — the 50/40 and 50/20 splits are a projection, and if premium share erodes the way the fee did, the answer changes. External: the book's own — the ad-supported model could be growing faster than the premium account, in which case the model we did not pick is the one gaining.
key.next: Put the same series against premium conversion, not just against the fee, before committing. Price the switching cost of moving models after launch, so the decoy is refused with a number rather than an argument.

en: Minto: the first sentence is the verdict itself — an action with a subject. A correct verdict arriving after the facts fails this line.
States that the ranking is a first-year figure while the decision has a longer horizon — the frame, not the arithmetic, is what is wrong.
Uses the trend in Block C explicitly, not as a general remark about competition.
Names the $5.1M lead being given up, rather than avoiding it.
Names the base difference — 1,800,000 against 300,000 — as the reason the surviving model is the wider one.
Refuses the launch-then-switch option, and says why.
Gives one internal and one external risk.
Sets its own block markers: conclusion, facts, risk, next step.
ru: Минто: первое предложение — сам вердикт, действием и с субъектом.
Сказано, что ранжирование — цифра первого года, а решение живёт дольше: неверна рамка, а не арифметика.
Тренд из блока C использован явно, а не как общая ремарка про конкуренцию.
Названа отдаваемая разница $5.1M, а не обойдена.
Названа разница баз — 1 800 000 против 300 000 — как причина.
Отвергнут вариант «запустить и потом переключиться», с обоснованием.
Назван один внутренний и один внешний риск.
Маркеры блоков расставлены самим кандидатом.

reference.en:
**Conclusion.** Kelvarno should launch on the premium-account model.

**Facts.** The note's arithmetic is right and its frame is not: **$25.7M** against **$20.6M** is a first-year comparison, and the model is chosen once for years. Block C says the paying-fee share and the fee itself have fallen since 2008 and faster since free competitors arrived in 2012 — that is the segment the winning model is built on. Premium gives up **$5.1M** in year one and stands on **1,800,000** users instead of **300,000**.

**Risk.** Internal: the premium conversion split is itself a projection and can erode the same way. External: the book's own — the ad-supported model could be growing faster than premium.

**Next step.** Run the same series against premium conversion before committing, and price the cost of switching models after launch so that "start on the fee and change later" is refused with a number.

**Source:** `9.-Stern-MCA-Casebook-2019`, Grad-U-Date, Questions 4–6 — base of 6,000,000; monthly fee 5% × $10 × 12 = $36.0M revenue and $25.7M profit; premium 30% × (50% × 40% + 50% × 20%) × $5 × 12 = $32.4M and $20.6M; advertising 40% × (50% × $0.75 + 50% × $1.25) × 12 = $28.8M and $16.4M; fixed costs $10,000,000 and $1 per member; and the guidance that the candidate should switch the recommendation from monthly fee to premium because "the portion of customers willing to pay a fee and the average fee paid have been rapidly decreasing since 2008".
